clue.text: A dangerous beast — and meaner at break

indicators.note: to break the words is to shatter them so their letters can be reassembled

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A warning about a savage animal that grows nastier when it breaks loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' tells you to rearrange MEANERAT, the letters of 'meaner at'; 'and' merely joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-eating tiger or shark is a classic example of a perilous wild animal.

clue.text: Monotonous scenery?

definitions.meaning: in theatre, a painted wooden frame forming part of the set

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the theatrical sense: a stage set is built from these painted panels.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull voice is described as lacking variation, and a stage panel of painted canvas bears the same short name.

clue.text: A form to do away with!

definitions.meaning: in some British schools a particular class or year group is called by this name

explanation.walkthrough: In some British public schools a 'form' (a class) between two others is called a Remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A school class at certain British schools carries this name, and the verb means to eliminate or take off.

clue.text: Army call-up

parts.note: not conscription but the bugle signal that calls soldiers up out of bed each morning

explanation.walkthrough: 'Call-up' suggests drafting recruits; here it is the morning bugle that gets troops up.
explanation.definitionFit: The morning bugle call in a military camp rouses soldiers from sleep.

clue.text: The record's being set straight by the old town

indicators.note: the jumbled words are put into proper order, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, with the S counted as a letter

explanation.surface: Someone correcting the historical record about an ancient settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being set straight' rearranges THERECORDS; the S of 'record's' counts. 'by the' is linking. DORCHESTER is the historic county town of Dorset in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorchester is a historic market settlement in Dorset with Roman origins.

clue.text: Heartless people returning fish and other food

indicators.note: the word people loses everything but its first and last letters
the fish's name is read backwards, as if coming back

parts.note: tuna is a fish

explanation.surface: Cruel folk come back from the sea with fish and other things to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' leaves PE from 'people'; 'returning' turns TUNA into ANUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundnut is a further edible item besides fish.

clue.text: Tiles are fixed before anything else

indicators.note: fixed in the sense of rigged or doctored, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A roofer's priority: the tiles go up first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fixed' rearranges TILESARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming at the very first point in time, ahead of all others.

clue.text: Jewellery for women in topmost position

definitions.text: Jewellery for women in topmost position

parts.words: Jewellery for women in topmost position
parts.note: ornaments worn by women which sit at the highest point of the body, on the head

explanation.walkthrough: 'Topmost position' sounds like rank or status, but means the top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Jewelled coronets are worn on top of the head.

clue.text: English poet and English epic poetry

parts.note: E again for English
Alexander Pope was an English poet
E again for English

explanation.surface: A bare list: an English poet and English epic verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope is the 18th-century poet Alexander Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: An epopee is an epic poem or the genre of heroic narrative verse.

clue.text: Inclined to be corrupt

explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is linking. 'Bent' as dishonest is British slang ('a bent copper').
explanation.definitionFit: Having a leaning towards something, and crooked in British slang.

clue.text: Place stone in a new setting, showing play of colour

indicators.note: a jeweller's word for remounting, used here for putting the letters in new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A jeweller resets a gem so it shimmers with colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a new setting' rearranges PLACESTONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridescent like an opal, with shifting milky colours.

clue.text: The chief's old — keeping quiet

indicators.note: one word holds another inside it, as a keeper holds something

parts.note: stale means old, not fresh
p, piano, is the musical abbreviation for quiet

explanation.surface: Gossip that the boss is elderly and keeping silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The chief's' looks like a person; it means the main item, as in a staple food. 'keeping' puts P inside STALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple is a principal or main item, as in a basic commodity.

clue.text: Stopped up to ten and collapsed

indicators.note: a collapse breaks things into a heap, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A boxer counted out: stopped at ten and down he went.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapsed' rearranges UPTOTENAND.
explanation.definitionFit: To terminate something is to have halted it for good.

clue.text: Complaints made by many males in small islands

indicators.note: one group of letters sits within another

parts.note: aits are small river islands
L is fifty in Roman numerals, taken as many
men are males

explanation.surface: Grumbles from crowds of men stuck on little islands.
explanation.walkthrough: AITS (or eyots) are small islands in a river, especially the Thames. 'made by' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaints in the medical sense are illnesses or disorders.

clue.text: Catch mount the wrong way, which is deplorable

indicators.note: both words are run backwards, against normal order

parts.note: a net is used to catch
a tor is a hill or rocky peak

explanation.surface: Someone tries to get onto a horse backwards, which is shameful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' turns NET+TOR into ROTTEN. A TOR is a rocky hill, common on Dartmoor in England. 'which is' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotten here is informal for very bad or contemptible.

clue.text: Is it essential to watch one's diet?

definitions.text: Is it essential to watch one's diet?

parts.words: Is it essential to watch one's diet?
parts.note: read as something to see with plus something to eat with: an organ of sight and a biting tool

explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' is eye and 'diet' suggests chewing; people say they'd give their eye teeth for something essential.
explanation.definitionFit: A canine is the upper pointed tooth beneath the eye.

clue.text: Fire the fellow at the end of December

parts.note: he refers to a man

indicators.note: the closing letters of the month's name are taken

explanation.surface: A man warming up at the close of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the end of December' supplies its last two letters, ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire in the British sense is a room-warming appliance.

clue.text: Left in the long grass, so it's said

parts.note: reed is a tall grass
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Something abandoned in tall grass, or so the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like abandoned, but it is the nautical word for the left side; 'in' puts it inside the tall grass. 'so' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Reported describes what is claimed or stated by others.

clue.text: A raptor's really big kill

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize
prey is an animal killed by another

explanation.surface: A hawk boasting of a huge catch.
explanation.walkthrough: OS (outsize) is a clothing abbreviation for very large. 's is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish-eating hawk is a bird of prey.

clue.text: The parsimony of the average head!

parts.note: mean is a type of average
ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A gibe about the stinginess of a typical headteacher.
explanation.walkthrough: NESS is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness. 'of the' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinginess is an unwillingness to spend.

clue.text: Dodges back inside as advised — a very wise decision

indicators.note: the letters are read in reverse order
the letters are found within the run of words

parts.words: as advised — a very wise decision

explanation.surface: Praise for a well-judged decision to sidestep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' hides SEDAVE in 'adviSED A VEry', and 'back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodge is to avoid or escape something cleverly.

clue.text: Pop back enveloped in dry wrap

indicators.note: one word is wrapped within another

parts.note: sere means dry or withered
pa is a father, pop

explanation.surface: Dad comes home wrapped in something dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the word for father around, and 'enveloped in' wraps the word for dry around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A serape is a Mexican shawl or blanket worn over the shoulders.

clue.text: Firm note cutting days off

indicators.note: one piece slices into the middle of another
off as in wrong or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: te is a note in tonic sol-fa

explanation.surface: A company's memo announcing cuts to days off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges the letters of 'days' to SADY; 'cutting' slips the sol-fa note into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Steady means stable and not wavering.

clue.text: Seafood as the principal part of a meal?

definitions.text: Seafood as the principal part of a meal?

parts.words: Seafood as the principal part of a meal?
parts.note: read as sea, the poetic word, plus a dish: the chief plate of a dinner

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is a poetic term for the sea, and a course is part of a meal, so 'Seafood' splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief dish of a dinner, served after the starter.

clue.text: Put up with a pain in the neck

definitions.meaning: tolerated, the past tense of bear

explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of endure, and a tedious person or thing.

clue.text: Not a square dance!

parts.note: a formal dance, but also something round rather than square

explanation.walkthrough: 'Square dance' is a real folk dance; here it means a dance that is not square but round.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand formal dance, and also a round object.

clue.text: Be a winger and get going!

parts.note: a tit is a small bird, a winged creature

explanation.surface: Telling a footballer to play on the wing and get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winger' looks like a football position but is a bird. 'and' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for go away, clear off.

clue.text: Off-peak caller

parts.note: not a cheap-rate phone user but an Alpine singer calling from the mountain top

explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-peak' suggests cheap phone rates; read it as from a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: An Alpine singer who warbles across the mountains.
